cls: Class IA antiarrhythmic (sodium-channel blocker) - cinchona alkaloid
quick: Quinidine sulfate 200-300 mg PO 3-4 times daily; quinidine gluconate ER 324-648 mg PO every 8-12 h
May take with food to reduce GI upset; avoid grapefruit juice and large diet changes
Crosses placenta; use only if benefit justifies risk - monitor neonate
Excreted in breast milk in small amounts; generally considered compatible with monitoring
Reduce dose in renal impairment; risk of accumulation - monitor levels
Reduce dose in hepatic impairment (extensively metabolised by CYP3A4)
Avoid - may potentiate hypotension and CNS effects
ECG (QT/QRS), serum levels, electrolytes (K, Mg), CBC, liver function
summary: Quinidine is a Class IA antiarrhythmic and cinchona alkaloid that blocks fast sodium channels (and potassium channels) to slow conduction and prolong repolarisation, used to convert and maintain sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation/flutter and to treat life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. Antiarrhythmic survival trials of Class IA agents show no mortality benefit and a potential for increased mortality, so use is reserved for arrhythmias judged life-threatening or markedly symptomatic. Key hazards are proarrhythmia (torsades de pointes from QT prolongation), cinchonism, thrombocytopenia, and many drug interactions.
indications: Conversion of atrial fibrillation/flutter to sinus rhythm and maintenance of sinus rhythm after conversion
Suppression of recurrent documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., sustained ventricular tachycardia)
Treatment of certain supraventricular and ventricular ectopy/tachyarrhythmias
Quinidine gluconate IV (where available) and oral quinidine used for severe/complicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria when IV artesunate is unavailable

dosage.d: Quinidine sulfate 200-300 mg PO 3-4 times daily
dosage.n: Conversion regimens individualised with ECG monitoring; give a test dose to detect idiosyncratic reaction

dosage.d: Quinidine gluconate extended-release 324-648 mg PO every 8-12 h
dosage.n: 324 mg gluconate approximately 202 mg quinidine base; titrate to effect/levels

dosage.d: Loading 6.25 mg base/kg (10 mg gluconate salt/kg) IV over 1-2 h, then 0.0125 mg base/kg/min infusion
dosage.n: Continuous ECG and BP, central monitoring; transition to oral antimalarial when able
Monitor plasma levels (therapeutic approximately 2-5 mcg/mL) and QT interval

admin: Take oral doses consistently with respect to food; swallow extended-release tablets whole - do not crush or chew
Consider a single small test dose before full therapy to detect idiosyncratic hypersensitivity
IV quinidine (malaria) must be given by slow infusion with continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring in a critical-care setting
Correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia before and during therapy
Obtain baseline and serial ECGs; stop if QRS widens >25% or QTc becomes markedly prolonged
moa: Quinidine blocks fast inward sodium channels (Class IA), slowing phase 0 depolarisation and conduction velocity, and also blocks the delayed-rectifier potassium current (IKr), prolonging action potential duration and the QT interval. It has vagolytic (anticholinergic) and alpha-adrenergic blocking properties that can increase AV conduction and lower blood pressure. As an antimalarial it is toxic to the erythrocytic stages of Plasmodium.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to quinidine, quinine or other cinchona alkaloids
Thrombocytopenia or other cytopenia attributable to quinidine/quinine
Complete AV block or marked QRS/QT prolongation without a functioning pacemaker
History of quinidine-associated torsades de pointes or long QT syndrome
relative: Concurrent QT-prolonging drugs or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors/digoxin
Untreated/incomplete heart block, sick sinus syndrome

preg: Quinidine crosses the placenta and reaches the fetal circulation. It has been used in pregnancy to treat maternal and fetal arrhythmias and malaria. Use only when the maternal benefit clearly justifies the potential fetal risk; monitor the neonate for arrhythmia and thrombocytopenia.
lact: Quinidine is excreted into breast milk in small amounts and infant plasma levels are generally low. It is usually considered compatible with breastfeeding, but observe the infant and avoid in infants at risk of arrhythmia or G6PD-related hemolysis.
renal: Quinidine is partly eliminated renally and accumulates in renal impairment. Reduce the dose and lengthen the dosing interval, and monitor plasma concentrations and the QT interval. Alkaline urine increases reabsorption and raises levels.
hepatic: Quinidine is extensively metabolised by hepatic CYP3A4. In hepatic impairment clearance falls and the half-life is prolonged; reduce the dose, monitor levels and watch for proarrhythmia and toxicity.

major: Other QT-prolonging drugs (sotalol, amiodarone, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, methadone) - additive torsades risk; avoid
Digoxin - quinidine raises digoxin levels markedly; halve digoxin dose and monitor
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir, grapefruit juice) raise quinidine levels; CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, phenobarbital) lower them
Quinidine inhibits CYP2D6, raising levels of many beta-blockers, tricyclics, codeine (reduces analgesia), and antiarrhythmics
moderate: Other Class I and Class III antiarrhythmics (additive conduction/repolarisation effects)
Verapamil, diltiazem (additive hypotension/conduction slowing; raise quinidine levels)
interactions.food: Grapefruit juice raises quinidine levels and prolongs QT - avoid; large changes in dietary acid/alkali load alter urinary excretion and levels
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - may add to hypotension and CNS depression and alter levels
interactions.diagnostics: Prolongs QRS and QT on ECG; can cause false elevation when interfering assays are used - interpret levels with the specific assay

serious: Torsades de pointes and other ventricular proarrhythmia (may occur at therapeutic levels)
Marked QT/QRS prolongation and conduction block
emergency: Torsades de pointes / ventricular fibrillation or syncope

monitoring: Baseline and serial ECG - QRS width and QTc; stop if QRS widens >25% or QTc markedly prolongs
Liver function tests and renal function
counsel: Take your dose at the same times each day; swallow long-acting tablets whole
Report ringing in the ears, blurred vision, severe diarrhea, fainting, palpitations, easy bruising or bleeding, or yellowing of skin/eyes
Avoid grapefruit juice and tell your doctor before starting any new medicine
Carry a list of your medicines - quinidine interacts with many drugs
Do not stop or change the dose without medical advice
pk: Oral 1-3 h to peak effect; IV effect within minutes
Plasma peak approximately 1.5-3 h (sulfate); 3-4 h (gluconate ER)
Approximately 6-8 h (longer in hepatic/renal impairment and the elderly)
Approximately 6-8 h (immediate release); longer with extended-release formulations
Store at room temperature 15-30 C, protected from light and moisture; keep tablets in original container
pearls: Class IA antiarrhythmics carry an antiarrhythmic-drug mortality context: trials show no survival benefit and possible increased mortality, so reserve for life-threatening or markedly symptomatic arrhythmias
Torsades can occur at therapeutic or even subtherapeutic levels - it is idiosyncratic, not dose-dependent; correct K and Mg first
Cinchonism (tinnitus, visual changes, headache) is an early warning sign of toxicity
Quinidine doubles digoxin levels - anticipate and reduce the digoxin dose
Its vagolytic effect can speed AV conduction in atrial flutter, so pre-treat with an AV-nodal blocker to avoid 1:1 conduction
missed: If you miss a dose take it as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for the next dose - then skip the missed dose. Never double up, because excess quinidine can cause dangerous heart rhythm changes. Resume the regular schedule.
overdose: Overdose causes severe QRS and QT widening, ventricular arrhythmias (including torsades), hypotension, seizures, cinchonism, and cardiovascular collapse. Management is supportive with continuous cardiac monitoring: sodium bicarbonate (sodium load) for QRS widening, magnesium and overdrive pacing/isoproterenol for torsades, IV fluids/vasopressors for hypotension, and treatment of seizures. Quinidine is highly protein-bound, so dialysis is of limited value; urinary alkalinisation should be avoided as it increases reabsorption.
